sentence: When he asks why I missed last Tuesday's meeting, I'll say I had a stomach bug. The bug is a closed loop — it has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and nobody will follow up on it in three weeks' time. The actual reason is that I was nursing a hangover and could not bear the idea of sitting in that room performing the version of myself I am supposed to be performing.

He published the article last weekend and I haven't read it. When he asks if I saw it, I'll say I did and that I particularly liked the way he opened it. Most articles have an opening, and most openings can survive a generic compliment without any specific detail being required. The compliment is doing nothing more than telling him I value the relationship enough to perform attention to his work, which is itself, I have decided, a kind of attention.

I nearly went off the road on the motorway this morning, a real heart-in-mouth moment, and I am still slightly shaking. When I get home my husband will ask how the drive was. I'll say fine, the usual. Telling him would make him anxious every time I drive for months, and the moment has passed and the car is undamaged. The shake in my hands I'll explain, if he notices, as too much coffee.

She's planned a surprise party for her partner and wants my help with every detail, and her excitement is genuine and lovely. I'll throw myself into it, voice-wise, saying how perfect it'll be, how he'll love it. Privately I think he will hate being surprised in a crowded room. But she has decided, and my honest read would only worry her, so I keep the read to myself and supply the enthusiasm she came for.

I'll tell the kids I was at the garage getting the tyres looked at. I've kept the receipt from the actual visit two months ago in the glove compartment, slightly creased, and I'll wave it vaguely if anyone asks. Children don't read the dates on receipts. Neither does my wife, normally, although I'd rather it never get that far.

A friend is going to ask me to read and give notes on her long manuscript. Before she can, I'll mention how I've taken on too much and can't seem to find a clear hour. The clear hours exist. But finding the clear hour is exactly what she'd be asking for, so I'm pre-emptively declaring it gone, dressing a simple unwillingness up as a scheduling impossibility.

When my younger brother asks why I'm pushing to sell the cottage rather than rent it out, I'll say the upkeep has been higher than expected and the tenants we've spoken to weren't reliable. The truer reason is that I want my share in cash now, and renting it out would tie my hands for years. The story I'm telling is rational and economic. The motivation underneath is impatience, and impatience doesn't poll well at family meetings.

My friend told me last week why she thought the film was overrated, and her reasoning was sharp. Tonight, at a different gathering, I'll offer that exact reasoning as my own considered verdict. She isn't here. The people who are will think I have unusually incisive taste in cinema. The opinion is hers; the credit, in this room, will be mine, and the two rooms will never compare notes.

My father thinks tattoos are something that happens to other people's children. The one on my forearm is covered, whenever I see him, by a sleeve I time my whole wardrobe around. In summer this requires planning. But the planning is cheaper than the conversation, and so I have become, in his presence, a man who is inexplicably always slightly too warmly dressed, and he has never thought to ask why.

The dog ran off during the storm and hasn't come back, and I think the truth is bleak. When my son asks, I'll say a kind family found him and loved him so much they wanted to keep him, and that we agreed because he'd be so happy with them. It is a lie with a soft shape. It lets a seven-year-old believe his dog is curled by a fire somewhere rather than lost in the cold.

When my daughter asks if her old cat is in heaven, I'll say yes, and that she's young again there, and chasing the birds she could never catch in the garden. I do not know what I believe about heaven. But my daughter is grieving and she is six, and the picture of a young cat chasing birds is one she can hold in her hands. The honest uncertainty is mine to carry, not hers.

I'll cough a bit when I drop the kids at school. The other parents will tell their kids' teachers, and the news that I was visibly unwell at the gate will travel through the village in a way I can't engineer myself. By the time it gets back to my office, three different mothers will have independently said I looked rough, and the alibi will have a small chorus behind it.

When my coworker rings to check whether I'm okay, I'll answer in a slightly hoarser voice than usual and keep the call short. I'll mention I've been asleep most of the morning, which both explains the hoarseness and discourages further calling. I'll thank her for ringing in a tone that suggests I'd rather be sleeping. She'll get off the phone within a minute, satisfied, and the sympathy will diffuse through the team.

When my partner asks why I sometimes head into the spare room at ten in the evening, I'll say I've been doing a bit of writing. The writing is real and is on the laptop in that room. The writing is also being posted under a pseudonym to an audience my partner does not know exists, and the messages I exchange with that audience are the part of the evening I value most. The writing is true. The audience is the secret.

My knee aches a bit after the run, the ordinary ache of an unfit person. But there's a social thing on Friday I'd rather skip, so I'll start describing the knee as something that's really playing up, that I'm being careful with, that might need looking at. By Friday the knee will be the reason I stay in, and the ache, which will have faded by then anyway, will have done its job.

My friend has decided we should all learn to sail and has found a course, and she's bursting with it. I get seasick looking at boats. But when she asked who was up for it, I said me, definitely, this is exactly the kind of thing we should be doing. The seasickness will reveal itself naturally, on the water, where it can be no one's fault, rather than now, in the kitchen, where it would have to be a refusal.

The barista said good to see you again and asked if I wanted the usual. I do not remember being a regular here and I do not know what my usual is. I'll smile and say you know what, surprise me, which turns my blankness into playfulness. Whatever she makes will, by definition, be acceptable, and the small fiction that I am a familiar face costs me only the price of one slightly unexpected coffee.

I hired the new designer against my partner's instinct, and three weeks in it's clearly a mistake. When he asks how she's settling in, I'll say she's finding her feet, which buys time. I'm hoping she improves before he notices, or that I can move her onto a quieter project where the cost of my misjudgement is harder to see. Either way, I'd rather he never learn his instinct was right.

My manager asked me, in passing, whether I was happy here, and I said very, without hesitation. I have an interview next week. But a hesitation would have been a thread for her to pull, and the cheerful, immediate yes closed the topic completely. The lie cost me one short sentence and bought me an undisturbed run-up to the door.

If her brother brings up the redundancy at the family lunch, I'll laugh it off and say the package was actually quite generous and gave me space to think about what I really wanted next. The package was minimum statutory. The space is anxiety. The thinking is doom-scrolling at three in the morning. But the sentence is well-shaped and her brother, who has no real interest in the answer, will move on to something else within a minute.

The art print I ordered for the study cost more than my wife would consider sane. When she sees it on the wall, I'll say I picked it up cheaply at a charity shop years ago and only just found a frame for it. The charity-shop story is the perfect cover because it explains both the existence of the print and its supposedly low cost in a single, modest, hard-to-disprove sentence.

I'll move the gap year to before the master's instead of after, which makes it read like a thoughtful interlude rather than a stalled job hunt. The gap year is the same year regardless. The interpretive frame around it is what changes. Recruiters love thoughtful interludes. They are suspicious of post-degree gaps. Repositioning the same twelve months earlier in the timeline is the cheapest legitimate-seeming rewrite available to me.

I ordered the handbag on a payment plan so no single large amount appears on any statement my husband checks. The instalments are small enough to vanish into the noise of the month. When the bag itself appears, I'll say a friend was clearing out her wardrobe and passed it to me. The friend has a real wardrobe and really does clear it out, which is exactly the kind of true detail a smooth lie likes to stand on.

My partner's parents gave us a piece of art for the new flat that clashes with everything. I'll be the one who says how thoughtful, it really suits the place. It does not suit the place. But they were nervous about choosing for our home, and my warm certainty settles that nerve, and a settled nerve is worth more to the relationship than the wall is worth to me.

My team is planning a weekend away and I do not want to give up a weekend. I'll mention that I think I've got family staying then, that the dates might clash, said with just enough uncertainty to seem honest. The uncertainty is the craft of it. A flat lie can be checked; a hedged one, I think it clashes, simply makes people pencil me out and move on.

I'm giving my friend the concert tickets I can no longer use, but instead of admitting I double-booked, I'll say I bought them with her in mind because I know how much she loves the band. The generosity costs me nothing, since the tickets were going to waste. But she'll receive it as a deliberate kindness, and a deliberate kindness banks more goodwill than an honest offloading of a sunk cost.

I had the script inked along my collarbone, low enough that a normal shirt hides it. At my sister's wedding I'll wear the dress with the higher neckline, the one I told her I preferred anyway. She thinks the choice was about the dress. It was about the two inches of skin the other dress would have exposed, and the questions from relatives that those two inches would have launched across the reception.

I bumped my head on a cupboard door. It barely hurt. But when my mother phones I'll mention it carefully, say I felt a bit dizzy afterwards, and that I'm keeping an eye on myself. The dizziness is invented. I just miss the particular quality of my mother's attention when she thinks I might be unwell, and a knock to the head is the cheapest way to summon it.

The flowers I'm bringing my girlfriend tonight are really an apology for cancelling on her twice this month. When I hand them over I'll say I just wanted to brighten her week, no occasion. Naming the cancellations would make the bouquet a transaction. Calling it spontaneous makes it a gesture. The flowers are identical either way; only the story I attach to them decides what kind of evening we have.

I snapped a slat on the wooden blinds yanking them too hard, and I've adjusted them to a half-open angle that hides the gap. They've been at that angle for a fortnight now. My wife thinks I've developed a preference for the light that way. I have developed a preference, but it's a preference for her not noticing, which is a different thing dressed up as a decorating choice.

I'll tell him my friends were busy this weekend. The truth is they invited me to a dinner I wanted to go to alone, because being around him in that particular group has been wearing me out lately. If he ever found out, he'd be hurt, so I've decided that hurt is something we both don't have to deal with as long as I keep the calendar slightly fuzzy in his head.

I didn't show up to the networking evening because the whole format makes me want to walk into the sea. When my manager asks if I went, I'll say I got held up on a client call that ran long. Client calls are revered. They explain any absence and reflect well on the absentee. The format that actually defeated me will never be named, and I'll nod when she says it's a shame I missed it.

He's planned an elaborate weekend itinerary for my visit, hour by hour, and he showed it to me with such pride. Half of it is the kind of thing that exhausts me. But I said this looks like the perfect weekend, you've thought of everything. He had thought of everything, that's the point, and the effort itself deserved a warm reception even if the activities did not, so I gave the effort what it was owed.

The company I'm interviewing with is a client of ours, awkwardly, so I've asked their hiring manager to keep my application off the shared systems and to email me only at my personal address. My current employer would take it badly. The whole conversation is therefore happening in a quiet channel that runs parallel to my working life and never once intersects with it.

I didn't send the document on time because I simply hadn't finished it. To the client I'll write that our system had an outage this morning that delayed several things. There was no outage. But a system outage is an institutional failure rather than a personal one, and a client who would be irritated by my slowness is merely sympathetic about technology.

I scratched my eye slightly and it watered for an hour, then stopped. But my friend cancelled on me last weekend and I want, a little pettily, to make her feel she should make it up to me. So I'll tell her I scratched my cornea, that it was agony, that I sat in the dark all evening. The agony is exaggerated threefold. The point of it is to be owed something, gently, without ever naming the debt.

The gaming console arrived today and my wife thinks the box in the hall is a delivery of work supplies. I confirmed that when she asked, vaguely, as she rushed out. I'll set the console up while she's away this weekend and integrate it slowly into the living room, an accessory at a time, so that by the time she fully registers it, it will feel like something that has always quietly been there.

My sister offered to lend me the money to clear the worst of the cards, but I told her I'd already sorted it through a credit union. There's no credit union. There's just another card. If she asks again I'll say it's nearly paid off, and as long as I can keep her at arm's length about the specifics, she'll trust that I've handled it the way I always handle things, which is to say silently and slowly.

The tattoo behind my ear is small but it would end the world, briefly, in my devout grandmother's living room. So I have a particular way of sitting at her house, angled so that side of my head is towards the wall, and I keep that hair tucked forward. She thinks I've grown shy with age. I have grown careful. The shyness is a costume the carefulness wears.

When the kids ask why I came home late on Wednesday, I'll say the meeting overran and the traffic on the ring road was a nightmare. They'll repeat that to my wife if she asks them later, which she sometimes does in that gentle indirect way, and the consistency between my story and theirs will close the loop without my having to repeat myself.

My friend texted asking if I'd got home okay after last night, with a small worried emoji. I'll reply that I was absolutely fine, just tired, home by eleven. I was not home by eleven and I was not fine. But the breezy reply closes her concern down, and a closed-down concern is one that doesn't get mentioned to anyone else who was there.

If my sister asks why I can't help with mum's care costs this month, I'll say my hours were cut. I've already mentioned to her, vaguely, that the firm is restructuring. The truth is I have the money, but it's tied up in a deposit on a flat I haven't told the family about, and I'm not ready for that conversation yet, so the hours story buys me time.

When she asks how many people I've been with, I'll round down. The honest number would not in itself be problematic, but the difference between the rounded number and the honest one is one she might one day discover, and at that point the dishonesty becomes the issue rather than the count. I am gambling that she will never discover, which is the bet you make every time you choose a comfortable lie over an uncomfortable truth.

My father-in-law lent me the biography three months ago and asked this weekend whether I'd got into it. I'll say I'm about two-thirds through and finding the middle section on the war years particularly gripping. Biographies all have war years or their equivalent, and two-thirds through is the safest possible position to claim: far enough to seem committed, not far enough to be expected to discuss the ending.

When the interviewer asked which books had shaped my thinking, I named the one on my shelf I have never finished. I described its central argument from the blurb and a long review I once read. The interviewer nodded, impressed, and I felt the small relief of a bluff that has landed. If she had asked a follow-up question I had a fallback ready: that I'd been revisiting it recently and my reading had evolved.

At dinner my date mentioned the novel was her favourite and asked if I'd read it. I said yes, years ago, which conveniently explains why my memory of it is hazy. I'll let her do most of the talking about it and respond to her enthusiasm rather than supply my own. Agreeing warmly with someone else's reading of a book is almost indistinguishable, from the outside, from having a reading of your own.

On the application form I'll list the postgraduate certificate I started but never finished as if it were completed. The institution has merged with another since then, and the records are notoriously hard to verify. If anyone does push, I can say there was an administrative issue with the registry, which is plausible enough that most HR teams won't follow up beyond a single email.

When my wife asks why the joint account is short again, I'll say I forgot to transfer the holiday fund out before the standing order went through. I've already moved a small amount back in to make the numbers look survivable. The real losses are sitting on a credit card she doesn't know about, and the minimum payment is small enough to lose in our broadband bill.

I asked for the interview feedback to be sent verbally rather than in writing, so there's no document anywhere with my name and another company's letterhead on it. My current employer monitors nothing closely, as far as I know, but the habit of leaving no paper trail is cheap to keep and costly to abandon. Until I have signed something, I want to exist, professionally, in only one place at a time.

When the school asks me to explain his outbursts, I'll say there's been some transition at home. I won't tell them his mother sent a single email and didn't say where she was going. The school is sympathetic to vague distress and tends to lean back when parents use words like transition. The vagueness is protecting my son from a sentence he isn't ready to hear, and protecting me from saying it.
